newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong shares close at record high, Tokyo slips.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shares close at record high, Tokyo slips.

text.p: European buyers pushed Hong Kong's Hang Seng index to a record high close on Wednesday, but in Tokyo shares slipped back amid investor caution ahead of October 20 general elections.
Elsewhere in Asia, Seoul's market added 2.53 percent on anticipation of an interest rate cut, while Bangkok, Jakarta and Sydney lost ground.
Traders said the Hang Seng finished up 143.81 points, or 1.19 percent, at 12,250.57, as large buy orders from Europe pushed prices higher in the last hour of trade.
The previous record close set by the blue chip index was 12,201.09 on January 4, 1994.
"European funds are getting in," said Ricky Tam, senior research analyst at Delta Asia Securities.

"Yesterday people tried to push the index down but it seems that it cannot break below 12,000 so people are changing their positions. In the futures market, a lot of big investors had short positions this morning and are changing to long positions," he said.
Miles Remington, sales trader at Crosby Securities, said the market had been quiet until European markets opened.
"We assume it must be from European buyers. The market was quiet until lunch time, then woke up in the second half when Europe becomes more active," he said.

Analysts noted a sharp rise in turnover during the afternoon session. Turnover totalled HK$6.21 billion (US$803.3 million) at the end of the day, compared to HK$2.99 billion during the morning session.
Brokers said the imminent general elections had dampened buyer enthusiasm. The key 225-share Nikkei average lost 167.70 points, or 0.80 percent, to finish at 20,870.83.
"Until we can paint a clearer picture of a new government, we won't be able to move much," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, senior analyst at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
Kaoru Ichikawa, a senior trader at Kokusai Securities Co Ltd, said the unclear political outlook had made investors wary.
Bolstered by across-the-board buying, Seoul's composite stock index rose 20.16 points to close provisionally at 817.78.

"Lower interest rates are the major theme in the market," said Lee Yon-suk, broker at Citicorp International. "But I expect no further steep rises on the index. After some consolidation, the market will show steady rises."
Analyst Hwang Chang-joong of LG Securities said investors believe a rate cut will help companies and improve market liquidity.

Economic planners and senior officials of the ruling New Korea Party have agreed in principle that money market rates would soon be lowered by one to two percent to help domestic companies boost international competitiveness.
Thai stocks ended slightly down in moderate trade on light foreign selling. The SET index slipped 6.90 points, or 0.72 percent, by the close to 949.44.
"Foreigners continued selling today, although local mutual funds entered the market and bought some stocks," said Somchai Trairattanapirom of Sitca Investment and Securities.
Jakarta share prices were lower but the downside was capped by bargain hunters, brokers said.
The composite index fell 1.47 percent, or 8.46 points, to close at 566.32 points.
The Australian sharemarket closed down after a slide in bank issues prompted investors to take profits.
The key All Ordinaries index, finished 21 points, or 0.90 percent, lower at 2,310.7.
At 10.42 GMT, the dollar was at 111.46/1.49 yen and 1.5295/99 marks.
Bullion ended at US$380.80/381.30, against New York's US$381.10/60 close.
SIMEX North Sea November Brent crude oil futures fell in late trading to $24.42 a barrel, down 16 cents from London's settlement.
